title: Object Detection
summary: Locating and classifying multiple objects per image — two-stage vs one-stage detectors, and how detection is scored.

slides.subTitle: Bounding boxes
slides.markdown: Classification answers "what is this image?"; detection answers "what objects are in this image, and where?" — potentially multiple objects, of different classes, at different scales. The output isn't a single label but a **set of predictions**, each a bounding box (typically x, y, width, height) plus a class label and a confidence score. This dual task — localization (getting the box right) and classification (getting the label right) — is why detection models are trained with a **combined loss**: a regression loss on box coordinates plus a classification loss on the label, summed and jointly optimized.

slides.subTitle: Proposing candidate regions
slides.markdown: Rather than predicting arbitrary box coordinates from nothing, most detectors tile the image with a dense grid of **anchor boxes** — predefined boxes of various sizes and aspect ratios at every grid location. The model then predicts, for each anchor, whether it contains an object and how to **adjust** that anchor's coordinates (small offsets) to better fit the actual object — a much easier learning problem than predicting raw coordinates from scratch, since the anchor gives the model a strong starting guess. Anchor sizes/ratios are usually chosen ahead of time based on the typical object shapes in the target dataset (e.g. wide anchors for cars, tall ones for pedestrians).

slides.subTitle: The R-CNN family — propose, then classify
slides.markdown: Two-stage detectors (R-CNN → Fast R-CNN → Faster R-CNN) split the job into two passes. **Stage 1**: a region proposal network scans the image and proposes a smaller set of candidate boxes likely to contain *some* object (without yet saying which class). **Stage 2**: each proposed region is cropped, resized, and run through a classifier to assign a class and refine the box. This separation lets the second stage focus its capacity only on plausible regions rather than the whole image, generally giving higher accuracy — at the cost of running two networks in sequence, which is slower than doing both jobs in one pass.

slides.subTitle: YOLO/SSD — a single pass
slides.markdown: One-stage detectors (YOLO, SSD) skip the separate proposal stage entirely: a single network looks at the whole image once and directly predicts, for every anchor location, a class and a box offset simultaneously. "You Only Look Once" is a literal description — no cropping-and-reclassifying step. This makes one-stage detectors substantially faster (often real-time, 30+ fps), at a historical cost in accuracy versus two-stage detectors, especially on small objects — though later YOLO versions have closed much of that gap through architectural improvements.

slides.subTitle: Accuracy vs speed
slides.markdown:
| | Two-stage (Faster R-CNN) | One-stage (YOLO/SSD) |
|---|---|---|
| Speed | Slower (~5-15 fps typical) | Faster (often 30+ fps, real-time) |
| Accuracy, esp. small objects | Historically higher | Historically lower, though the gap has narrowed |
| Pipeline complexity | Two networks, more moving parts | Single network, simpler to deploy |
| Best fit | Offline batch analysis, accuracy-critical (medical, security review) | Real-time apps (autonomous driving, live video, mobile) |

How to decide: if the product genuinely needs real-time inference (self-driving perception, live camera apps), one-stage is usually the right call even at some accuracy cost; if you're processing images offline and accuracy is paramount, two-stage detectors are still a strong choice.

slides.subTitle: Cleaning up overlapping box predictions
slides.markdown: Detectors typically predict many overlapping boxes for the same object (multiple anchors near the object all fire). **Non-Max Suppression (NMS)** cleans this up: sort predicted boxes for a class by confidence score, keep the highest-confidence box, discard any other box that overlaps it above an IoU threshold (commonly 0.5), then repeat with the next-highest remaining box. Without NMS, a single object would show up as a cluster of near-duplicate boxes in the output, which is why NMS is a standard post-processing step in essentially every detector, not an optional add-on.

slides.subTitle: Intersection over Union as the localization metric
slides.markdown: **IoU** measures how well a predicted box matches a ground-truth box: the area of their overlap divided by the area of their union. IoU = 1 means a perfect match; IoU = 0 means no overlap at all. It's the fundamental building block used in two places: **NMS** (deciding which overlapping predictions are "the same object") and **evaluation** (deciding whether a prediction "counts" as correctly localizing an object, typically requiring IoU ≥ 0.5 against ground truth). Understanding IoU is a prerequisite for understanding both how detectors clean up their own output and how detection quality gets scored.

slides.subTitle: The standard detection evaluation metric
slides.markdown: **mAP (mean Average Precision)** is the standard way to score a detector across all classes and confidence thresholds at once. For each class: rank predictions by confidence, compute precision and recall at every threshold, and take the area under that precision-recall curve — this is **Average Precision (AP)** for that class, and it accounts for both false positives and false negatives simultaneously, unlike accuracy. Average AP across all classes to get **mAP**. You'll often see "mAP@0.5" or "mAP@[0.5:0.95]" — the number after the @ is the IoU threshold used to decide whether a predicted box counts as a correct match, with the range notation meaning it's averaged across several thresholds for a stricter, more holistic score.
